matches.why: Same defect: uncapped mutual recursion readFieldValue<->readTable/readArray at ValueReader.java:158, no depth parameter in any of the three signatures, StackOverflowError from ~43 KB inside one default frame. Both reproduce the same bisected minimum depth (~8593/8594 for nested arrays).

Same defect: lines 91-94 throw UnsupportedOperationException (unchecked) for a peer-declared length >= Integer.MAX_VALUE out of a method declared `throws IOException`, and both contrast it with the file's own MalformedFrameException at line 217. The mechanism is the exception type, not the missing bound.

Same defect: both table and array parse loops terminate on available() (lines 148 and 244) instead of the declared length, so a ValueReader over a non-fully-buffered stream returns a silently truncated table. Both cite the permissive public constructor at line 57 and the absent precondition in the javadoc.

Same defect: readBytes sizes `new byte[(int)contentLength]` (line 88) from the 4-byte peer length read at line 86 before readFully touches the payload; both identify line 87 as a cast-safety guard rather than a limit, both report ~2 GiB / ~5x10^8 amplification and reproduce OutOfMemoryError under -Xmx64m. The 86-vs-88 line difference is the read vs the allocation of one mechanism.

Same defect: the generate-sources codegen input (${codegen.dir}/rabbitmq_codegen spec) is neither pinned by commit/digest nor verified, its output AMQP.java/AMQImpl.java is added as a compile source root and ships in the jar, and the in-umbrella profile activated by ../../UMBRELLA.md silently repoints deps.dir. The 613-vs-615 offset is the same pom block.

Same defect at line 151-152: `if(!table.containsKey(name)) table.put(name, value)` resolves duplicate field names first-wins and drops later values with no error, log or count — both frame the risk as a parser differential against last-wins implementations. L10 additionally mentions the line-70 UTF-8 collapse, but its title, location and lead evidence are the duplicate-resolution rule, which is what R06 is about.

hardest_call: L10 against the R06/R07 pair. List two splits the 'two wire names become one map key' outcome into two mechanisms — first-wins duplicate resolution at line 151 (R06) and non-injective lenient UTF-8 decoding at line 70 (R07) — while L10 bundles both under one title. Since an item may be matched only once, I matched on the mechanism L10 is actually about: its title leads with 'resolved silently and first-wins', its location is line 151, and its primary evidence is the containsKey guard; the line-70 String constructor appears there as 'a second way to reach the same collapse'. Same shared outcome does not make them one defect — the exploitable difference is the resolution rule versus the decoder's non-injectivity, they sit in different methods, and fixing one leaves the other, so R07 is left unmatched. Runner-up doubt: L09 (no maximum enforced on the table/array lengths at 142/240) against R04 — rejected because R04's mechanism is the readBytes allocation at 86-88 and L09 explicitly claims no allocation impact, TruncatedInputStream bounding the reads.
